Deer
DEER
n. (a wild ruminant; in the AV, the fallow deer)
Hebrew yachmur, the fallow deer or roebuck, from a root meaning red or ruddy. Old English deor, which once meant any wild animal and narrowed over time to this family. It appears in the list of clean wild game Israel might eat.

Biblical Definition

The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois. The list is the positive side of the dietary law, and its presence is easy to overlook. Having forbidden the hare, the camel, the coney, and the swine, Moses names seven wild animals Israel was free to hunt and eat. The law was not a regime of scarcity; it drew a line and left a great deal of ground inside it. These are all wild game, taken by hunting rather than raised, which also means the ordinary Israelite had access to meat beyond his flocks. The deer family runs through Scripture in the language of longing and of sure-footedness. The most famous instance is the psalm that gave the church one of its enduring pictures of spiritual thirst: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. Habakkuk uses the same animal for stability in hard country — he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. And Isaiah promises that in the restoration the lame man shall leap as an hart. A creature known for thirst, for speed, and for footing on broken ground turns out to be a natural figure for the life of faith, and Scripture uses it for all three.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a quadruped of the genus Cervus, of several species, as the stag or red deer, the fallow deer, and the roebuck.

expand to see more

DEER, n. A quadruped of the genus Cervus, of several species, as the stag or red deer, the fallow deer, and the roebuck.

DEER, n. These animals are wild, and hunted in the chase; they are remarkable for fleetness.

HART, n. A stag or male deer, an animal of the cervine genus.

ROEBUCK, n. A species of deer, the smallest of the cervine genus, with erect cylindrical branched horns.

CHAMOIS, n. A species of goat, whose skin is made into soft leather.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 14:5 — "The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois."

Deuteronomy 14:7 — "Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you."

Psalm 42:1 — "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God."

Isaiah 35:6 — "Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert."

Modern Corruption

The law is remembered only for its prohibitions, and the goodness of creaturely provision within it is forgotten; Deuteronomy names what Israel could freely eat before naming what it could not.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape of the law itself. Deuteronomy 14 begins with a list of what may be eaten and then gives the exclusions, and the order is not accidental; the same pattern governs Eden, where every tree was given and one was withheld. A religion remembered chiefly by its prohibitions has been remembered badly. Paul writes against exactly that distortion when he names as a doctrine of devils the commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving, and adds that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving.

The second matter is the use Scripture makes of this animal, which repays attention in a culture that treats spiritual desire as either sentiment or technique. The hart panting after water brooks is an image of thirst under duress — the psalm is written by a man whose tears have been his meat day and night and who is being asked, Where is thy God? Longing for God in the Bible is most often depicted in drought rather than in plenty. Habakkuk's hinds' feet come at the end of a book about invasion, and Isaiah's leaping hart belongs to a promise made to a lame man in a desert. The figure consistently belongs to people in hard country.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yachmur (H3180), the fallow deer; ayyal (H354), a hart or stag; tsebi (H6643), a roebuck or gazelle; ayyalah (H355), a hind.

expand to see more

Hebrew yachmur (H3180) — the fallow deer; named among the clean wild game.

Hebrew ayyal (H354) — a hart, a stag; the animal of Psalm 42 and Isaiah 35.

Hebrew tsebi (H6643) — a roebuck, a gazelle; also the word for beauty or glory.

Hebrew ayyalah (H355) — a hind; hinds' feet in Habakkuk and Psalm 18.

Hebrew arag (H6165) — to long for, to pant; as the hart panteth.

Usage

"“the hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer” — what Israel could freely eat."

"“as the hart panteth after the water brooks” — thirst under duress."

"“Then shall the lame man leap as an hart” — the promise of restoration."
